page_hint: Ch 15, §5 Common Mistakes, bullet 'Using scaled-dot-product attention without FlashAttention' (printed page not determinable from chunk)
quoted_clause: For long contexts (9,200+ tokens) the quadratic memory cost of SDPA (O(L²)) dominates the FLOP cost.
observed: This bullet asserts that SDPA's quadratic cost dominates the FLOP cost at 9.2K tokens. The chapter's own §3 computes the opposite: the attention term is ≈2.2×10¹⁴ FLOPs at L=9,200, which is ≈17% of the parameter-matmul FLOPs (2NL = 1.288×10¹⁵) and ≈15% of total forward FLOPs (case ii, 1.5099 PFLOP), and ≈8.6% / ≈8% under the causal triangle (case iii, 1.3989 PFLOP). A reader who trusts the bullet will conclude that attention FLOPs dominate long-context prefill, which the chapter's arithmetic refutes.
evidence: Independent rederivation from the chapter's own inputs: attention = 4·L²·d_model·n_layers = 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 × 80 = 2.2188×10¹⁴ FLOPs. Parameter matmul = 2 × 70×10⁹ × 9,200 = 1.288×10¹⁵. Ratio = 17.2%. Total = 1.5099×10¹⁵ → attention share = 14.7%. Causal triangle: 1.1094×10¹⁴ → 8.6% of 2NL, 7.9% of total. All three figures match §3 exactly, so the bullet is the outlier.
root_cause: The bullet conflates the memory-traffic argument (which is FlashAttention's actual motivation) with a FLOP-dominance claim, and was written without reconciling against §3's arithmetic. The two claims are also different in kind: bytes and FLOPs are not comparable without a machine-balance factor.
correction: Rewrite the bullet's first sentence to: 'For long contexts the quadratic *memory traffic* of SDPA — materializing the L×L score matrix — dominates its cost, while its FLOP cost is ≈15% of total forward FLOPs at 9.2K (§3; ≈8% under a causal mask). FlashAttention's gain is therefore an I/O gain, not a FLOP reduction.' Keep the rest of the bullet (it already says 'pays off specifically when memory-bound').
acceptance_test: The bullet's FLOP claim must equal §3's 15% (case ii) / 8% (case iii) figures; a reader who recomputes 4·L²·d·n_layers ÷ (2NL + attention) at L=9,200 must find the same number printed in the bullet, and no sentence in Ch 15 may claim attention dominates FLOPs at 9.2K.

page_hint: Ch 15, §8 mini-case (queueing-delay and throughput figures) and §4 Measurement ('A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps'); scope note at chapter head
quoted_clause: drops from 320 ms (single host, batch-1) to 140 ms (dual host, continuous batch), and token throughput rises from ~8.5K to 70,000 tokens/s
observed: The mini-case's operating point is physically inconsistent with the chapter's own capacity-deficit arithmetic. The mini-case inherits the deployment's traffic profile (12.5/50 rps) but quotes queueing delays and a serving throughput that cannot exist at that offered load on one or two hosts. §4's benchmark protocol has the same defect: it prescribes running 40 rps on the single host, which the chapter itself shows is 6.5× over the host's prefill ceiling.
evidence: Host prefill ceiling (linear-only, 100% MFU) = 7.912×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token = 56,514 tok/s. Offered prefill demand: 12.5 rps × 9,200 = 115,000 tok/s → 2.03× over; 50 rps → 460,000 tok/s → 8.14× over; 40 rps → 368,000 tok/s → 6.51× over (the chapter's own figure). Batch-1 single host: 9,200 tokens in 1.08 s → 0.93 rps capacity vs 12.5 rps offered → 13.4× over, so a p95 queueing delay of 320 ms is impossible (the queue grows without bound). Offered token rate at 12.5 rps = 115,000 + 3,750 = 118,750 tok/s vs a two-host ceiling of 113,000 tok/s (linear-only) → the quoted 70,000 tok/s is *below* offered demand, i.e. the system is not keeping up. Under the alternative reading (a saturation test), queueing delay is unbounded, not 140 ms. Both readings fail.
root_cause: The mini-case never states the offered load of the benchmark it reports. It borrows the deployment's traffic profile for context while quoting numbers that are only coherent at a much lower load, and the §4 protocol was written before the chapter established the 6.5× prefill deficit.
correction: State the benchmark's offered load explicitly in both §4 and §8, and reconcile the numbers with the deficit arithmetic. Either (a) re-label the mini-case as a saturation/sweep test with the offered load stated and the queueing-delay figures marked as measured under saturation, or (b) re-derive the 320/140 ms and 8.5K/70,000 figures at a load the host can actually sustain (≤ ~2 rps for one host, ≤ ~4 rps for two). In §4, replace 'runs 40 rps' with a load the host can serve, or state explicitly that the 40 rps run is a saturation test whose queue is expected to grow.
acceptance_test: Every throughput and latency figure in §4 and §8 carries an explicit offered load; recomputing prefill demand ÷ host ceiling at that load yields ≤1, or the text explicitly states the system is saturated and the queue unbounded. A reader must not be able to compute a 13× overload next to a 320 ms p95 queueing delay.

page_hint: Ch 15, 'Two Mechanisms, Read as Mechanisms' → 'Speculative decoding' paragraph; and the Optimization Decision Map row 'high TPOT/ITL + HBM bandwidth saturated'
quoted_clause: quantization, batching up, speculative decoding, smaller active params, more bandwidth
observed: The chapter never states the condition under which speculative decoding actually reduces weight-stream traffic, and the decision map places it in precisely the regime where it does not help. Decode at batch B streams the full weight set once per step, so bytes/token = W/B. Speculative decoding with acceptance length k streams the weights once per k+1 tokens, so bytes/token = W/(k+1). The traffic saving is positive only when k+1 > B. At the chapter's own batch-32 test point (§4) with a typical k of 4, speculative decoding reduces bytes/token by zero while adding draft-model cost and verification overhead. This also puts the map in direct tension with §6, which recommends continuous batching (large B) as the primary decode lever.
evidence: W = 140 GB (FP16 70B). Batch-32 decode: 140/32 = 4.4 GB/token. Speculative with k=4: 140/5 = 28 GB/token — worse than batch-32 decode. Batch-1 decode: 140 GB/token vs 28 GB/token — a 5× saving. The saving therefore exists only in the low-batch regime, which is the opposite of the 'HBM bandwidth saturated' symptom the map attaches it to.
root_cause: The speculative-decoding mechanism was described in isolation from the batch dimension that the same chapter makes central, and the decision map's 'evidence / measurement' column omits decode batch size, so the reader cannot see the precondition.
correction: Add the batch condition to the mechanism paragraph: 'The saving exists only while the decode batch is smaller than the expected acceptance length k+1: at batch B the weights are already streamed once per step for B sequences (W/B bytes per token), so speculative decoding can only help when k+1 > B. At large batch, where the chapter's own continuous-batching recommendation puts the system, speculative decoding reduces weight traffic by nothing and adds draft cost.' Add 'current decode batch size vs expected acceptance length' to the map's evidence column and annotate the row accordingly.
acceptance_test: The mechanism paragraph contains the inequality k+1 > B (or an equivalent statement); the map's evidence column lists decode batch size; a reader must be able to conclude from the chapter alone that speculative decoding does not help at batch 32.

page_hint: Ch 15, §3 Worked Example, 'Attention FLOP comparison' paragraph
quoted_clause: Attention is two matmuls per token per head — Q·$K^{T}$ then ·V — each a multiply-accumulate of L²·d, so in FLOPs (2 per MAC) the per-layer cost is ≈ 4 × L² × d_model
observed: The derivation is mis-stated. For a single query token, Q·Kᵀ is (1×d)·(d×L) = L·d MACs and (QKᵀ)·V is (1×L)·(L×d) = L·d MACs, i.e. 4·L·d FLOPs per token per head. L²·d is the cost for all L query positions in one head, not per token. The final formula 4·L²·d_model per layer is correct, but it does not follow from the sentence as written, and a reader following the printed derivation literally gets a factor of L wrong.
evidence: Per token per head: 2 matmuls × L·d MACs × 2 FLOPs/MAC = 4·L·d = 4 × 9,200 × 128 = 4.71×10⁶ FLOPs. Across L tokens and 64 heads: 4·L²·d_model = 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 2.773×10¹² per layer — matches the printed ≈2.8×10¹². Per-head sequence figure 4 × 9,200² × 128 = 4.33×10¹⁰ also matches the printed ≈4.3×10¹⁰. So only the 'per token' qualifier is wrong.
root_cause: The derivation sentence was written at the sequence level but labeled per token; the correct per-token and per-sequence quantities were never separated.
correction: Rewrite: 'Attention is two matmuls per head — Q·Kᵀ then ·V — each L²·d MACs for the whole sequence (equivalently 4·L·d FLOPs per token per head); with 2 FLOPs per MAC and n_heads heads, the per-layer cost is 4·L²·d_model.'
acceptance_test: A reader following the printed derivation reproduces 4·L²·d_model per layer with no factor-of-L discrepancy, and the per-token and per-sequence quantities are separately stated.

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 'Dominant Bottleneck' column (Light and Peak rows) vs. §3 Worked Example peak analysis
observed: The bottleneck column is not derived from the chapter's own arithmetic and contradicts §3 in two ways. (a) The Peak row ('KV + Inter-GPU bandwidth') omits the prefill compute deficit, which §3 identifies as the primary peak signal (6.5× over host peak), and introduces 'Inter-GPU bandwidth', a bottleneck this chapter never analyzes — there is no TP, collective, or multi-GPU content in Ch 15. The table's own note claims the column 'reflects the roofline logic of Chapter 8', which the numbers do not support.

Remove 'Inter-GPU bandwidth' from this table or replace it with the prefill compute deficit.

page_hint: Ch 15, §6 Architecture Consequence, decision (1)
quoted_clause: (1) FlashAttention‑2 as the default attention kernel, fused with RoPE and QKV projection to minimize HBM transactions
observed: FlashAttention-2 is an attention kernel: it takes Q, K, V as inputs and performs tiled attention with an online softmax. It does not fuse the QKV projection GEMM or the RoPE application into the attention kernel in its standard form. The sentence conflates attention-kernel fusion with GEMM-level fusion and with a separate RoPE-fusion choice, and it contradicts §3's careful framing of FlashAttention as an attention-I/O mechanism (tiling, online softmax, no materialized L×L matrix).
evidence: §3's own description of FlashAttention contains no projection or RoPE fusion; the chapter's Fig 15.1 caption likewise describes only tiled attention with online softmax. The QKV-projection fusion and the RoPE fusion are separate engineering choices made by the serving engine around the attention kernel.
root_cause: Conflation of 'fused attention' with 'fused attention + fused QKV GEMM + fused RoPE', which are three distinct decisions with distinct effects on HBM traffic.
correction: Split the decision into its components: '(1) FlashAttention-2 as the default attention kernel (attention-I/O fusion: tiled, online softmax, no materialized L×L score matrix); separately, fuse the three QKV projections into a single GEMM, and fuse RoPE into the attention prologue where the engine supports it.'
acceptance_test: The decision names which component performs each fusion; no sentence attributes QKV-projection or RoPE fusion to FlashAttention-2 itself; the description matches §3's account of the kernel.

page_hint: Ch 15, §2 Mental Model, token-reuse paragraph
quoted_clause: when many users share similar prompt prefixes, the KV cache can be partially shared, reducing memory traffic
observed: Prefix reuse eliminates redundant prefill computation and redundant KV allocation for the shared prefix. It does not reduce the KV bytes that must be read from HBM during decode for that prefix — decode reads the full K/V history of every sequence at every step regardless of whether the prefix was computed or reused. As written, the sentence can lead the reader to expect a decode-time bandwidth saving from prefix caching, which is the mechanism the chapter elsewhere (decision map, §6) correctly attributes to batching and quantization.
evidence: Decode attention reads the sequence's entire K/V history per step; the prefix's K/V must be resident and read whether it was just computed or restored from a cache. The savings from prefix reuse are (a) prefill FLOPs for the shared prefix and (b) KV capacity for the shared prefix.
root_cause: Conflation of 'avoid recomputation' with 'avoid re-reading', a distinction the chapter's own §4 measurement paragraph makes elsewhere ('compare the bytes transferred per request').
correction: Rewrite: 'when many users share similar prompt prefixes, the shared prefix's KV need not be recomputed or re-allocated, which removes prefill FLOPs and KV capacity; the KV bytes for that prefix are still read during decode, so the saving is in compute and capacity, not in decode-time traffic.'
acceptance_test: The sentence names prefill FLOPs and KV capacity as the savings and makes no claim about a decode-time traffic reduction; the claim is consistent with the decision map's placement of prefix caching under prefill.

page_hint: Ch 16, §2 Mental Model, second bullet ('Follow the token, not the GPU')
quoted_clause: Two systems with the same card count can differ 10× in cost per request if one has 3× the goodput per card, better utilization, or no idle coasting.

The 'or' list implies compounding factors without showing the composition, in a section whose stated purpose is to 'keep the arithmetic honest'.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Mode 2 — cloud GPU instances (rent, occupancy-input priced)', 'Default paid-occupancy ASSUMPTION' paragraph; also Table 16-1 row 'B. Cloud, default paid-occupancy input'; also 'Reading the result' paragraph. Page not determinable from chunk.
quoted_clause: The canonical default bills **6 × 730 = 4,380 host-hours → $87,600/month → $14.04 per 1,000 requests** (14.038461538461538 exact). This is an explicit illustrative occupancy INPUT: it is **not a measured duty cycle, not a load-duration integral, not a guaranteed lower bound, not a complete warm-plus-burst forecast, and not a proven feasible serving schedule**
observed: The default cloud occupancy input bills exactly 6 hosts for the entire month. The chapter's own screens make 6 hosts the *average* (10 rps) requirement and 21 hosts the *peak* (40 rps) requirement; the per-host admitted-rate ceiling is C/W = 17/8.6 = 1.9767 req/s, so 6 hosts can admit at most 6 × 1.9767 ≈ 11.9 req/s — under one third of the canonical 40 rps peak. The chapter never states this arithmetic. Its caveats describe the input as 'unmeasured' and 'not a proven feasible serving schedule', which understates the defect: the configuration is not merely unmeasured, it is arithmetically incapable of serving the stated peak. The $14.04/1K line is nevertheless the default row of Table 16-1, the basis of the '~1.8' self-host-to-cloud ratio, and the line the 'When each wins' section uses to say cloud wins.
evidence: 6 × 1.9767 = 11.86 req/s < 40 rps peak. The chapter's own mid-case example ('~6 reserved warm hosts + ~15 burst hosts held for ~4 peak hours/day') confirms that the 4,380 host-hour default is the warm pool only, with no burst term. The chapter's mid-case arithmetic (6 × 730 × $20 + 15 × 4 h × 30 d × $20 = $87,600 + $36,000 = $123,600) sits between the two named endpoints, confirming the default omits the burst.
root_cause: The occupancy input was chosen as 'the average host count' without checking it against the peak requirement, and the caveat language was written to cover 'unmeasured' rather than 'infeasible'. The gap then propagates into the headline ratio and the mode-ranking prose.
correction: State the arithmetic in the Default paid-occupancy ASSUMPTION paragraph and in Table 16-1's status cell: '6 hosts × 1.9767 req/s ≈ 11.9 rps < the canonical 40 rps peak — this configuration cannot serve the canonical peak; it is priced only as a lower-bound occupancy illustration.' Then either relabel the row 'B₀ — occupancy input, peak-infeasible (lower bound only)' and add the burst term to the default, or keep the row and add a sentence in 'Reading the result' that the $14.04/1K line is not a serviceable configuration for the canonical workload and cannot be read as 'cloud is cheaper at 6.24M'.
acceptance_test: The rendered text contains the inequality 6 × 1.9767 ≈ 11.9 rps < 40 rps adjacent to the $87,600 figure; Table 16-1's status cell for that row states the configuration is peak-infeasible; and the 'Reading the result' paragraph no longer presents $14.04/1K as a comparable alternative without that qualifier.

page_hint: Ch 16 — opening ('Size the fleet first, then price it'); the sizing-screen table; 'Parametric sensitivity is the durable form', bullet 'Fleet size'.
quoted_clause: We therefore size the fleet first (Ch 17) and price it second. … **Independent prefill screen — case (ii) full-square conservative** (×1.1723 on case (i)) … so **which FLOP-counting case is stated decides whether the compute screen (19), the KV screen (21), or the compute screen again (22) governs the peak**

Keep the 'size first, then price' framing either way, but make the reader able to evaluate the case choice.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Mode 3 — managed inference API' cost equation; the 'Independent prefill screen' rows of the sizing table; the floor-17 KV computation in 'Step 1 — fleet size'.
observed: The chapter never states the canonical request's token composition. Three screens depend on it and each uses a different total: the KV screen uses 9,500 tokens/request, the prefill screen charges 9,200 tokens/request, and the API cost line uses 9,200 input + 300 output. The chunk's internal evidence is consistent with a 9,200-token prompt plus 300 generated tokens (a 'prefill' screen that charges 9,200 tokens/request; a 1.08 s prefill / 7.5 s decode split implying ~8,500 tok/s prefill and ~40 tok/s decode; 9,500 = 9,200 + 300). But the book's canonical workload is also described elsewhere as 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200 tokens, under which the API line would be 0.002 × 1.2 + 0.008 × 8.0 = $0.0664/request — a 3.2× swing that reverses the chapter's 'self-host sits above the API at 6.24M' conclusion and moves the API break-even from ~7.5M to ~2.35M. The reader cannot resolve this from the chapter.
evidence: 0.002 × 1.2 + 0.008 × 8.0 = 0.0024 + 0.064 = $0.0664/req → $66.4/1K → 6.24M × 0.0664 = $414,336/mo; 155,816.93 / 0.0664 = 2,346,637 req/mo. Under the 9,200/300 reading the printed $0.0208 is correct. The chapter supplies no statement of I and O in tokens, so neither reading can be confirmed from the text.
root_cause: The chapter borrows canonical token counts from Ch 4/Ch 17 without restating the split, and the API line is the only place in the chapter where the input/output split changes the answer by more than 3×.
correction: State the canonical request shape explicitly in this chapter (e.g. 'the canonical request carries a 9,200-token prompt and generates 300 tokens; 9,500 tokens of KV per request'), and annotate the API equation with 'I = 9,200 tokens, O = 300 tokens'. Reconcile against design/canonical-workload.yaml; if the canonical is in fact 1,200 in / 8,000 out, recompute the API line, the $129,792/mo figure, the $20.8/1K cell, the $15–25/1K band and every break-even in the chapter.
acceptance_test: The chapter states I and O in tokens next to the API equation and the stated split matches design/canonical-workload.yaml and the 9,500-token KV figure; a reader can recompute $0.0208/request from the stated I, O and prices without consulting another chapter.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Treat both provisioning policies explicitly' paragraph; provisioning-policy table, last column.
quoted_clause: The capacity-planning rule (Ch 17's authoritative provisioning-policy table, **Table 17-1**) is N = ⌈λ·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare with u = 0.70 and ρ = 0.95 **independent** (u × ρ = 0.665, not nested) … at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy case (ii) gives **⌈21.81/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34 hosts** against **32** for KV-only
observed: u = 0.70 is a KV-slot occupancy target and ρ = 0.95 a scheduling factor; the formula's denominator C is a slot count. The 34-host row applies the same ÷0.665 derate to the case (ii) *compute* screen, whose 'C' is a token rate (19,780 tok/s/host), not a slot count. The chapter never says what u and ρ mean for a compute screen, so the 34-host and 32-host rows are presented as the same policy applied twice when they are not the same lever.
evidence: 21.81/0.665 = 32.80 → 33, +1 = 34; the KV-only row is 344/11.305 = 30.43 → 31, +1 = 32. The arithmetic is correct; the semantics of the derate for a compute-bound screen are unstated, and the compute screen already carries a 35% MFU assumption that is itself the headroom lever.
root_cause: A single provisioning formula is reused across two different resource screens without distinguishing what the utilization factor derates in each.
correction: State explicitly what u and ρ derate in each case (slot occupancy for the KV screen; headroom against the 35% MFU assumption for the compute screen), and note that the compute-screen derate is a different quantity from the KV-slot derate even though the arithmetic is identical. If the compute screen should not be derated at all, say so and give the resulting host count.
acceptance_test: The text states in one sentence the meaning of u and ρ for each of the two screens, and a reader can explain why the 34-host and 32-host rows differ by two hosts rather than assuming the same policy was applied twice.

page_hint: Ch 16 — 'Parametric multi-region worksheet' table, rows 2, 3 and 8.
quoted_clause: | 2 | Failover load | the surviving region must carry 100% of λ_peak = 40 rps | NOT SIZED | … | 3 | Warmed capacity per region | N_region = ⌈λ_region·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (Table 17-1 formula, applied per region) | NOT SIZED (depends on rows 1–2) | … | 8 | Incremental cost | extra regions + replication + routing/egress — on the order of ≥2× the single-region fleet on the capacity-duplication term alone (above) | NOT PRICED |
observed: Row 3 sizes each region from its *share* λ_region, but row 2 requires the surviving region to carry 100% of λ_peak, and row 8's ≥2× figure only follows if every region is sized for 100% of peak. As written, a reader who fills row 3 with λ_region = α·40 sizes each region for its share and obtains a fleet smaller than one region sized for peak — contradicting rows 2 and 8.
evidence: With α = 0.5, row 3 gives two regions each sized for 20 rps; the surviving region then admits only ~20 rps against the 40 rps required by row 2. Sizing each region for 40 rps gives 2 × 21 = 42 hosts, which is exactly where '≥2×' comes from.
root_cause: The worksheet parameterizes traffic share and failover load as independent rows without stating that the per-region sizing basis is the failover load, not the share.
correction: Add an explicit row (or amend row 3) stating the per-region sizing basis: 'each region is sized for λ_peak = 40 rps (the failover load), not for its share λ_region; λ_region determines only the traffic split, not the provisioned capacity', and note that this is what produces the ≥2× capacity term.
acceptance_test: Filling rows 1–8 of the worksheet with any α yields a per-region host count that satisfies row 2 (surviving region clears 40 rps) and a total consistent with row 8's ≥2× statement.

page_hint: Ch 17 §17.6 'Failover and redundancy'
quoted_clause: With N ≥ 2, the fleet provides automatic failover: if one host crashes, the LB routes its traffic to the remaining N−1 hosts, reducing capacity by 1/N (N to N−1 hosts). observed: The example contradicts the chapter's own provisioning model. Everywhere else in Ch 17 the fleet is provisioned with an N-1 spare (31 working + 1 = 32 total), so a single host loss is absorbed by the spare and the residual capacity is 100% of the working count, not N-1/N. The N = 4 -> 75% example describes a fleet without a spare, which is not the fleet the chapter sizes. The paragraph also leaves the reader with the impression that N must be chosen for residual-capacity reasons, when the chapter's own arithmetic already buys that property with one spare host.
evidence: §17.6 and Table 17-2: 31 working + 1 spare = 32 total; the N-1 row adds one spare host to every count.
root_cause: The failover paragraph was written before the N-1 provisioning rule was adopted and was not updated.
correction: Rewrite the paragraph in terms of the chapter's model: with the N-1 spare provisioned, a single host loss leaves the working count intact and the residual capacity is 100% of the working fleet; the residual-capacity question only arises for a second failure or for a region loss, which the multi-region caveat already covers. Keep the N = 4 / N = 6 arithmetic only if it is explicitly framed as the no-spare case.
acceptance_test: The failover paragraph's arithmetic uses the same N-1 provisioning model as the sizing sections, or explicitly states that it describes a no-spare fleet.

page_hint: Ch 17 §17.5 Common Mistakes #1
quoted_clause: each turn adds ~800 tokens of context, which linearly reduces concurrent‑request capacity.
observed: The relationship is stated with the wrong functional form. Per-request KV grows linearly in turns (I(T) = 9,200 + 865T + 300), but per-host concurrent capacity C = KV_budget / (kappa x I(T)) falls as the reciprocal of I(T), not linearly. The chapter's own numbers show this: C = 17 at T = 0 and C = 13 at T = 3, a 24% reduction for a 27% growth in context - the capacity curve is hyperbolic, and the flattening matters for the reader's intuition about how much more damage additional turns do.
root_cause: Loose phrasing of a reciprocal relationship.
correction: Rewrite as 'each turn adds ~865 tokens of context, which raises per-request KV and reduces per-host concurrent capacity in inverse proportion (C = KV_budget / (kappa x I(T)))'.
acceptance_test: The statement of how turns affect capacity matches the formula the chapter uses elsewhere.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.7 'What We Still Don't Know', third bullet
quoted_clause: **Cross-model distillation opportunities.** Can a 70B 4-bit model be distilled from a 70B FP16 teacher without quality loss, effectively lowering the cost floor? Empirical work needed.
observed: The bullet conflates two different mechanisms. Quantization reduces bit-width of an existing model; distillation trains a new, usually smaller, student model. 'A 70B 4-bit model distilled from a 70B FP16 teacher' is not a well-formed distillation setup - the student would be a different (smaller) model, and the 4-bit part is a separate, already-solved question. The cost-floor claim is also misattributed: quantization already lowers the per-token cost floor (the chapter's own table shows $2.50 -> $0.15/1M), so distillation's contribution is a further reduction in parameter count, not in bit-width.

root_cause: Two adjacent cost-reduction ideas were merged into one open question.
correction: Rewrite as two distinct questions: (a) does a smaller student distilled from a 70B FP16 teacher reach the quality bar that currently forces requests to the FP16 tier, and what is its serving cost per token; (b) separately, what quality is lost by quantizing the distilled student. Keep the quantization question out of the distillation bullet.
acceptance_test: The §18.7 bullet names one mechanism, and the cost-floor claim it makes is consistent with the §18.3.2 table.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.5 Common Mistakes #4
quoted_clause: **Over‑provisioning the top tier.** Keeping a full FP16 GPU idle "just in case" is expensive. Keep just enough capacity for the tail (≈10% of peak rps) and route the rest.
observed: The rule is stated without the arithmetic that makes it actionable, and the chapter has the arithmetic available. At the canonical peak, 10% of 40 rps is 4 rps; with C = 17 and W = 8.6 s a host serves 17/8.6 = 1.98 rps, so the FP16 tail needs 3 hosts at full utilization (5 at the 70% x 95% policy) - not 'just enough' in the abstract, and not one host as the mini-case's '2 GPUs reserved' might suggest. The reader is told to size the tail but is given no method for doing it.
